title: Carnot’s Perfect Heat Engine: The Second Law of Thermodynamics Restated
lead: A heat engine can never be perfectly efficient, so the question that remains is how efficient it can be. Sadi Carnot answered it in 1824 with a cycle made only of reversible processes, two isothermal and two adiabatic, which is the most efficient cycle possible between two given temperatures. Its efficiency depends on nothing but those two temperatures, and no real engine, with its friction and other dissipative processes, can quite reach it.
objectives: Calculate maximum theoretical efficiency of a nuclear reactor.
Explain how dissipative processes affect the ideal Carnot engine.
summary_html:
• The Carnot cycle is a theoretical cycle that is the most efficient cyclical process possible. Any engine using the Carnot cycle, which uses only reversible processes (adiabatic and isothermal), is known as a Carnot engine.
  • Any engine that uses the Carnot cycle enjoys the maximum theoretical efficiency.
  • While Carnot engines are ideal engines, in reality, no engine achieves Carnot’s theoretical maximum efficiency, since dissipative processes, such as friction, play a role. Carnot cycles without heat loss may be possible at absolute zero, but this has never been seen in nature.

figures.original_caption: This novelty toy, known as the drinking bird, is an example of Carnot’s engine. It contains methylene chloride (mixed with a dye) in the abdomen, which boils at a very low temperature—about 100 °F. To operate, one gets the bird’s head wet. As the water evaporates, fluid moves up into the head, causing the bird to become top-heavy and dip forward back into the water. This cools down the methylene chloride in the head, and it moves back into the abdomen, causing the bird to become bottom heavy and tip up. Except for a very small input of energy—the original head-wetting—the bird becomes a perpetual motion machine of sorts. (credit: Arabesk.nl, Wikimedia Commons)

PV diagram for a Carnot cycle, employing only reversible isothermal and adiabatic processes. Heat transfer Q_h occurs into the working substance during the isothermal path AB, which takes place at constant temperature T_h. Heat transfer Q_c occurs out of the working substance during the isothermal path CD, which takes place at constant temperature T_c. The net work output W equals the area inside the path ABCDA. Also shown is a schematic of a Carnot engine operating between hot and cold reservoirs at temperatures T_h and T_c. Any heat engine using reversible processes and operating between these two temperatures will have the same maximum efficiency as the Carnot engine.

Schematic diagram of a pressurized water nuclear reactor and the steam turbines that convert work into electrical energy. Heat exchange is used to generate steam, in part to avoid contamination of the generators with radioactivity. Two turbines are used because this is less expensive than operating a single generator that produces the same amount of electrical energy. The steam is condensed to liquid before being returned to the heat exchanger, to keep exit steam pressure low and aid the flow of steam through the turbines (equivalent to using a lower-temperature cold reservoir). The considerable energy associated with condensation must be dissipated into the local environment; in this example, a cooling tower is used so there is no direct heat transfer to an aquatic environment. (Note that the water going to the cooling tower does not come into contact with the steam flowing over the turbines.)

(a) A nuclear power station (credit: BlatantWorld.com) and (b) a coal-fired power station. Both have cooling towers in which water evaporates into the environment, representing Q_c. The nuclear reactor, which supplies Q_h, is housed inside the dome-shaped containment buildings. (credit: Robert & Mihaela Vicol, publicphoto.org)

Real heat engines are less efficient than Carnot engines. (a) Real engines use irreversible processes, reducing the heat transfer to work. Solid lines represent the actual process; the dashed lines are what a Carnot engine would do between the same two reservoirs. (b) Friction and other dissipative processes in the output mechanisms of a heat engine convert some of its work output into heat transfer to the environment.

exercises.prompt: Think about the drinking bird at the beginning of this section (Figure 15.20). Although the bird enjoys the theoretical maximum efficiency possible, if left to its own devices over time, the bird will cease “drinking.” What are some of the dissipative processes that might cause the bird’s motion to cease?

answer.solution: The bird runs as long as its head is cooler than its abdomen, and that difference is kept up by water evaporating from the head. Once the glass of water is empty, or the felt on the head dries out, there is no more evaporation, no temperature difference, and no engine. Even while the water lasts, irreversible processes are at work in the toy itself. Friction at the pivot and air resistance against the swinging body turn some of the small work output into heat transfer to the surroundings, and the fluid rubs against the glass as it moves up and down the neck. Heat transfer through the glass also warms the head and cools the abdomen a little toward the room temperature, which narrows the difference the engine runs on. Each of these is a dissipative process of the kind the section names, and each makes the bird less than the perfect Carnot engine it is often said to be.

exercises.prompt: Can improved engineering and materials be employed in heat engines to reduce heat transfer into the environment? Can they eliminate heat transfer into the environment entirely?

answer.solution: Yes to the first question and no to the second. Better engineering reduces the dissipative processes, such as friction and turbulence, that make a real engine less efficient than a Carnot engine between the same two temperatures, and better materials let the hot reservoir run hotter, which raises the Carnot efficiency $\text{Eff}_{\text{C}} = 1 - \kTempc/\kTemph$ itself. Both reduce the heat transfer $\kQC$ to the environment for a given work output. But no engineering can remove $\kQC$ altogether, because the second law of thermodynamics in its Carnot form says that even a perfect engine has an efficiency of only $1 - \kTempc/\kTemph$, and that is 100% only if the cold reservoir is at absolute zero, which is impossible. Some heat transfer into the environment is required by the law, not by the quality of the machine.

exercises.prompt: Does the second law of thermodynamics alter the conservation of energy principle?

answer.solution: No. Energy is conserved in every process a heat engine carries out: the heat transfer $\kQH$ that enters the engine in a cycle comes out again as the work $\kW$ and the heat transfer $\kQC$, so that $\kW = \kQH - \kQC$, and the first law of thermodynamics is obeyed exactly. The second law says something the first does not, namely which of the energy-conserving processes actually happen and how much of $\kQH$ can become work. A process in which all of $\kQH$ became work would conserve energy perfectly well, and the second law forbids it anyway. So the second law does not alter the conservation of energy; it adds a further restriction on top of it.

exercises.prompt: A certain gasoline engine has an efficiency of 30.0%. What would the hot reservoir temperature be for a Carnot engine having that efficiency, if it operates with a cold reservoir temperature of $200^\circ\text{C}$?

answer.hint: Convert the cold reservoir temperature to kelvins, solve $\text{Eff}_{\text{C}} = 1 - \kTempc/\kTemph$ for $\kTemph$, and convert the answer back to degrees Celsius.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the hot reservoir temperature of a Carnot engine that has an efficiency of 42.0% and a cold reservoir temperature of $27.0^\circ\text{C}$? (b) What must the hot reservoir temperature be for a real heat engine that achieves 0.700 of the maximum efficiency, but still has an efficiency of 42.0% (and a cold reservoir at $27.0^\circ\text{C}$)? (c) Does your answer imply practical limits to the efficiency of car gasoline engines?

parts.hint: With $\kTempc = 300\ \text{K}$, solve $0.420 = 1 - 300\ \text{K}/\kTemph$ for $\kTemph$ and convert to degrees Celsius.
If the real engine reaches only 0.700 of the maximum, the Carnot efficiency between its reservoirs must be $0.420/0.700 = 0.600$; find the hot reservoir temperature that gives that.

answer.solution: (a) $244^\circ\text{C}$ (b) $477^\circ\text{C}$ (c) Yes, since automobiles engines cannot get too hot without overheating, their efficiency is limited.

exercises.prompt: Practical steam engines utilize $450^\circ\text{C}$ steam, which is later exhausted at $270^\circ\text{C}$. (a) What is the maximum efficiency that such a heat engine can have? (b) Since $270^\circ\text{C}$ steam is still quite hot, a second steam engine is sometimes operated using the exhaust of the first. What is the maximum efficiency of the second engine if its exhaust has a temperature of $150^\circ\text{C}$? (c) What is the overall efficiency of the two engines? (d) Show that this is the same efficiency as a single Carnot engine operating between $450^\circ\text{C}$ and $150^\circ\text{C}$. Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategies for Thermodynamics.

parts.hint: The first engine runs between 723 K and 543 K.
The second engine’s hot reservoir is the first engine’s exhaust, 543 K, and its cold reservoir is 423 K.

The heat transfer that reaches the second engine is what the first one did not turn into work, so the fraction of the original heat transfer that is not converted by either is $(1 - \text{Eff}_1)(1 - \text{Eff}_2)$.

answer.solution: (a) $\text{Eff}_{1} = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{c,1}}}{T_{\text{h,1}}} = 1 - \frac{543\ \text{K}}{723\ \text{K}} = 0.249\ \text{or}\ 24.9\%$ (b) $\text{Eff}_{2} = 1 - \frac{423\ \text{K}}{543\ \text{K}} = 0.221\ \text{or}\ 22.1\%$ (c) $\text{Eff}_{1} = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{c,1}}}{T_{\text{h,1}}} \Rightarrow T_{\text{c,1}} = T_{\text{h,1}}(1 - \text{Eff}_{1})$; similarly, $T_{\text{c,2}} = T_{\text{h,2}}(1 - \text{Eff}_{2})$; using $T_{\text{h,2}} = T_{\text{c,1}}$ in the above equation gives $T_{\text{c,2}} = T_{\text{h,1}}(1 - \text{Eff}_{1})(1 - \text{Eff}_{2}) \equiv T_{\text{h,1}}(1 - \text{Eff}_{\text{overall}})$, $\therefore (1 - \text{Eff}_{\text{overall}}) = (1 - \text{Eff}_{1})(1 - \text{Eff}_{2})$, $\text{Eff}_{\text{overall}} = 1 - (1 - 0.249)(1 - 0.221) = 41.5\%$ (d) $\text{Eff}_{\text{overall}} = 1 - \frac{423\ \text{K}}{723\ \text{K}} = 0.415\ \text{or}\ 41.5\%$

exercises.prompt: Would you be willing to financially back an inventor who is marketing a device that she claims has 25 kJ of heat transfer at 600 K, has heat transfer to the environment at 300 K, and does 12 kJ of work? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: The heat transfer to the cold reservoir is $\kQC = \kQH - \kW = 25\ \text{kJ} - 12\ \text{kJ} = 13\ \text{kJ}$, so the efficiency is $\text{Eff} = 1 - \frac{\kQC}{\kQH} = 1 - \frac{13\ \text{kJ}}{25\ \text{kJ}} = 0.48$. The Carnot efficiency is $\text{Eff}_{\text{C}} = 1 - \frac{\kTempc}{\kTemph} = 1 - \frac{300\ \text{K}}{600\ \text{K}} = 0.50$. The actual efficiency is 96% of the Carnot efficiency, which is much higher than the best-ever achieved of about 70%, so her scheme is likely to be fraudulent.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the cold reservoir temperature of a steam engine that uses hot steam at $450^\circ\text{C}$ and has a Carnot efficiency of 0.700. (b) What is unreasonable about the temperature? (c) Which premise is unreasonable?

answer.hint: Solve $\text{Eff}_{\text{C}} = 1 - \kTempc/\kTemph$ for $\kTempc$ with $\kTemph = 723\ \text{K}$, then convert to degrees Celsius and ask whether a steam engine could exhaust into anything that cold.
answer.solution: (a) $-56.3^\circ\text{C}$ (b) The temperature is too cold for the output of a steam engine (the local environment). It is below the freezing point of water. (c) The assumed efficiency is too high.
